title: Suffering can teach, because Christ descended below it all
setting: Joseph Smith was a prisoner in the jail at Liberty, Missouri, when this text was written. It comes from a letter to Bishop Edward Partridge and the Church dated about 22 March 1839. Joseph likely dictated it, and fellow prisoner Alexander McRae wrote it out. In the letter the voice shifts from the prisoners to words addressed to Joseph as “my son”. By then Joseph had been held in Liberty for nearly four months.
summary: The voice tells Joseph that the ends of the earth will ask about his name. Fools will mock him, but the pure in heart will seek his counsel. Traitors will not turn his people against him. It then lists trials: false accusation, being torn from family, prison, and a sentence of death. It pictures his six-year-old son clinging to him and asking why he cannot stay. All these things, it says, “shall give thee experience” and be for his good. It says the Son of Man has descended below them all. Joseph should hold on, for his days are known and God will be with him.

contextNote.title: Measured against Christ’s descent
contextNote.text: Verses 5–7 list hardship after hardship that could fall on Joseph, up to “the very jaws of hell”. It claims all of them can give experience and work for his good. Verse 8 gives the reason in a short question: “Art thou greater than he?” The Son of Man, it says, “hath descended below them all”. Joseph’s suffering is placed beneath Christ’s, not outside God’s knowledge. Verse 9 then draws the result: hold on, because the enemies’ bounds and Joseph’s days are set. In this passage, descending means taking on suffering deeper than any Joseph faced.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 121–123 teaches that the Savior understands every trial. How does the question in verse 8 change the meaning of the hardships listed in verses 5–7?

jsp.title: Letter to Edward Partridge and the Church, circa 22 March 1839

reviewNote: Read all 9 verses. Official heading: word of the Lord to Joseph Smith in Liberty jail, excerpted from the epistle of about 22 March 1839. JSP historical introduction read for the dating, McRae as scribe of draft and fair copy, and the shifting voice. The six-year-old son in v. 6 is Joseph Smith III (born November 1832), not named in the text. Nearly four months counts from 1 December 1838; Joseph had been in custody since 31 October 1838. Fact-check 2026-10-12: contextNote now says verses 5–7 (not verse 7 alone) list the hardships; summary attributes the Son of Man's descent to the text.
